metadata.title: Bridging the Pixel Gap in Browser Automation.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: how do you turn the coordinates Claude reports after looking at a screenshot into a click that lands on your real screen? Lands the carry-out that Claude's coordinates live in a resized copy of your screen, and the ratio multiply is what maps them back.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (screenshot click at 728,409 on a 1456x819 image, scaled by the viewport/1456,819 ratio to land at 1280,720 on a real 2560x1440 screen)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes Claude's click coordinates land on your screen's exact pixels. They don't. Claude's vision encoder resizes every screenshot to a fixed canvas before it looks — the numbers it reports live in that resized canvas, not yours. So how do you map them back to a real pixel on your actual screen?

beats.narration_text: The browser tool screenshots your screen and hands the image to Claude. But Claude's vision encoder only accepts one size for 16:9 input: 1456 by 819 pixels. It resizes every screenshot down to that before looking. One input pipeline, not one per screen resolution — that's the design choice. The cost: every coordinate Claude reports lives in that resized canvas, not yours. Take the numbers straight and you miss the button.

shot.new_visual_element: A small screenshot rectangle and a larger real-screen rectangle; a dot maps straight across at the same raw numbers and misses

production_viz.label: Same raw pixel, wrong screen
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a small outlined rectangle labelled '1456 × 819 — what Claude sees' on cream, with a terracotta dot inside it and a target ring nearby. Right: a larger outlined rectangle labelled 'YOUR REAL SCREEN', proportioned differently. An arrow carries the dot's raw (x,y) straight across; on the right rectangle the dot lands away from the target ring, marked with a cross.

beats.narration_text: The concrete case. Claude's canvas is 1456 by 819, and it reports a click at 728, 409 — dead center of what it sees. Your real viewport is 2560 by 1440 — same 16:9, but nearly twice the size on each axis. Take (728, 409) as-is on your actual screen and you land near the top-left corner. 728 out of 2560 is a quarter across, not the middle. Same numbers, different canvas, different physical spot.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - screenshot rect labelled 1456x819 with a dot at (728,409); the same raw pixel plotted on the larger 2560x1440 rect lands near the corner, marked with a miss

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - 728,409 on the wrong canvas
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left rectangle labelled '1456 × 819' with a terracotta dot at dead center, captioned '(728, 409)'. Right rectangle labelled '2560 × 1440' (visibly larger, same aspect). The exact same (728, 409) coordinate is plotted on the right rectangle, landing near its top-left corner with a cross mark, far from a target ring near center. THIS EXACT PAIR OF RECTANGLES RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: The fix is the inverse of the resize. Multiply Claude's x by viewport_w over 1456, and its y by viewport_h over 819 — you're just undoing the shrink, one axis at a time. Then clamp both to the screen's edges, because Claude occasionally reports one pixel outside its own canvas and you don't want to click into nothing. coordinate_scaling.py runs the whole thing in twenty lines.

shot.new_visual_element: Formula card: real_x = x * (viewport_w / 1456), real_y = y * (viewport_h / 819), then a clamp note

production_viz.label: The inverse ratio
production_viz.mechanic: Two formula lines build in ink mono on cream: 'real_x = x × (viewport_w / 1456)' then 'real_y = y × (viewport_h / 819)'. Beneath, a smaller line in terracotta: 'clamp to [0, viewport_w-1] / [0, viewport_h-1]'. A small caption bottom-right: 'coordinate_scaling.py — 20 lines'.

beats.narration_text: Back to the anchor. 2560 over 1456 is about 1.76, and 1440 over 819 is also 1.76 — because both rectangles are 16:9, so the width ratio and the height ratio have to match. Multiply 728 and 409 by 1.76 and you land at 1280, 720 — dead center of the real screen. The one-multiply fix works because the aspect ratios line up. Hand the encoder a non-16:9 screenshot and it resizes to a different fixed size — different divisors, from a lookup table, not this same multiply.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - same two rectangles; the scaled dot now lands on the target; a mismatched-aspect rectangle beside it is struck through

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - scaled, and lands
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 RECTANGLE PAIR RETURNS, identical. This time the (728, 409) dot is carried across with the ratio applied, landing exactly on the target ring at '(1280, 720)' inside the 2560×1440 rectangle, marked with a check. Off to the side, a third, differently-proportioned rectangle (not 16:9) appears with a dashed outline and a strike-through, captioned 'different lookup table' in ink — the caveat, not the main case.

beats.narration_text: Claude's coordinates live in a resized copy of your screen — multiply by the inverse ratio back to real pixels, or the click lands nowhere near the button.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Claude reports a click on a 1456 by 819 screenshot, but my screen is 1920 by 1080. Write me a scaling function, clamped to the viewport, and walk me through what breaks if the screen isn't 16:9. Then go deeper: what does the encoder do with a non-16:9 screenshot — does it fall back to a different fixed size, and where's the table of those sizes? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: Claude reports click coordinates on a 1456×819 resized screenshot, but my real screen is 1920×1080. Write me a Python function that takes Claude's (x, y) and returns the real-screen click coordinate, clamped to the viewport. Then walk me through exactly what breaks if my screen isn't 16:9 — where does the one-multiply assumption fail, and what has to replace it?
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what does the vision encoder do with a non-16:9 screenshot — does it letterbox, or fall back to a different fixed input size from a lookup table? Find the table and the rule for choosing a size.
